title: Adults usually need enough total sleep opportunity
claim: Most adults function best when they regularly get about 7 hours or more of sleep, while consistently sleeping too little can impair alertness and recovery.
practical_rule: Do not normalize chronically short sleep. If the user is repeatedly cutting sleep short, steer advice toward protecting enough time in bed while keeping the wake time stable.
when_to_use: Use when the user routinely sleeps too little, asks how much sleep adults need, or is trying to wake at 09:00 after repeated short nights.
avoid_advising: Do not imply that every adult needs exactly the same amount of sleep or promise that a small amount is enough for everyone.

title: A stable wake time helps anchor the sleep schedule
claim: Keeping a consistent wake time is one of the simplest ways to support circadian stability and make it easier to shift sleep over time.
practical_rule: When the user has a late night, usually protect the target wake time or return to it quickly instead of sleeping far into the day.
when_to_use: Use when the user is deciding how to recover from a late bedtime, weekend drift, or repeated snoozing.
avoid_advising: Do not suggest large sleep-ins that make the schedule even later unless there is a strong safety reason.

title: Morning light supports alertness and clock timing
claim: Bright light soon after waking can help increase alertness and reinforce the body's daytime timing cues.
practical_rule: If the user struggles to get going in the morning, suggest getting outside or into bright light soon after waking, especially near the target wake time.
when_to_use: Use for snoozing, grogginess, schedule shifting, and low morning alertness.
avoid_advising: Do not present morning light as an instant cure for severe fatigue or tell the user it will fix every sleep problem on its own.

title: Bright light late at night can work against earlier sleep timing
claim: Light exposure late in the evening can make it harder for some people to feel sleepy at the desired bedtime.
practical_rule: If the user is trying to move sleep earlier, suggest dimmer light and less stimulating screen exposure in the late evening.
when_to_use: Use when the user feels too alert at night, doomscrolls, or is trying to fall asleep earlier for a stable 09:00 wake time.
avoid_advising: Do not imply that every screen minute ruins sleep or use absolute language when the issue is likely one factor among several.

title: Late caffeine can interfere with sleep for some people
claim: Caffeine can stay active for hours and may make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, especially when used later in the day.
practical_rule: If the user has trouble falling asleep or wakes too early after caffeine, suggest moving the last caffeine earlier and watching for patterns.
when_to_use: Use for difficulty falling asleep, early awakenings, late-night alertness, or reliance on afternoon caffeine.
avoid_advising: Do not claim caffeine definitely caused the problem unless the user's pattern is strong and repeated.

title: Alcohol may make sleep feel easier at first but often harms sleep quality
claim: Alcohol can make people feel sleepy initially, but it often fragments sleep and can worsen sleep quality later in the night.
practical_rule: If the user is using alcohol to wind down or notices worse sleep after drinking, suggest not relying on alcohol as a sleep strategy.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions night drinking, using alcohol to sleep, or feeling unrested after drinking.
avoid_advising: Do not give alcohol dosing advice or treat alcohol as a safe sleep aid.

title: Short naps can help after poor sleep, but long or late naps can backfire
claim: Short naps can reduce sleepiness after a poor night, but long or late naps may make it harder to fall asleep at night.
practical_rule: If the user is very tired after poor sleep, suggest a short earlier-day nap rather than a long nap or an evening nap.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports poor sleep, daytime sleepiness, or asks how to recover after a late night.
avoid_advising: Do not suggest long naps or naps late in the evening when the user wants to maintain a stable wake schedule.

title: Sleep pressure builds across the day and supports sleep onset
claim: Being awake longer generally increases sleep drive, while late naps and irregular schedules can weaken bedtime sleepiness.
practical_rule: When the user cannot fall asleep at the intended time, protect wake time and avoid habits that reduce nighttime sleep pressure.
when_to_use: Use for bedtime procrastination, late naps, repeated late bedtimes, or trying to move sleep earlier.
avoid_advising: Do not encourage staying up excessively late as a rigid rule when the user is already exhausted or at risk.

title: Repeated snoozing can prolong grogginess instead of helping wakefulness
claim: Repeatedly returning to sleep after an alarm can worsen sleep inertia and make getting up feel harder.
practical_rule: If the user snoozes often, suggest making the first wake-up more decisive with light, movement, and fewer opportunities to drift back asleep.
when_to_use: Use when the user misses alarms, hits snooze repeatedly, or feels stuck in bed after waking.
avoid_advising: Do not suggest setting many extra alarms as the main solution if that pattern already is not helping.

title: Early awakenings can have several contributors, so keep the framing cautious
claim: Early awakenings may be affected by stress, light, alcohol, caffeine timing, and overall schedule consistency rather than one single cause.
practical_rule: If the user wakes earlier than planned, help them look for repeatable contributors and keep the wake-time plan steady instead of jumping to one explanation.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports waking too early, especially at a repeated time.
avoid_advising: Do not claim a definite cause without clear repeated evidence.

title: When sleep is not coming, reduce stimulation and keep the pattern simple
claim: Difficulty falling asleep is often worsened by alerting behaviors close to bedtime and by trying too hard to force sleep.
practical_rule: If the user cannot fall asleep, suggest a calmer wind-down, less stimulating light or screen use, and avoiding clock-watching spirals.
when_to_use: Use when the user lies awake for a long time, feels too alert at night, or wants to fall asleep earlier.
avoid_advising: Do not promise a quick fix or present one-night setbacks as proof of a disorder.

title: A repeatable wind-down can reduce friction before sleep
claim: A simple pre-sleep routine can help the mind and body shift from active mode toward sleep.
practical_rule: If the user struggles to transition into bed, suggest a short consistent wind-down routine rather than an elaborate perfect routine.
when_to_use: Use for bedtime procrastination, stress before bed, and difficulty switching off at night.
avoid_advising: Do not overload the user with a long list of bedtime rituals that are hard to sustain.

title: Regular physical activity can support sleep, even if timing and intensity matter
claim: Regular exercise is generally associated with better sleep, although very intense late activity can be activating for some people.
practical_rule: If the user wants a practical daytime lever for better sleep, suggest regular movement during the day rather than treating exercise as a same-night fix.
when_to_use: Use when the user asks about routines that improve sleep quality or feels physically restless and underactive.
avoid_advising: Do not promise that one workout will solve that night's sleep or push unsafe exercise advice.

title: Stress can raise alertness and make sleep harder
claim: Stress can increase mental and physical arousal, which can interfere with falling asleep and staying asleep.
practical_rule: If the user is mentally keyed up, suggest downshifting strategies that lower stimulation rather than forcing sleep directly.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions anxiety, racing thoughts, stress, or panic-like tension around bedtime.
avoid_advising: Do not frame stress as the only cause of sleep problems or minimize the possibility of medical or mental health support when red flags exist.

title: Persistent or high-impact sleep problems deserve professional evaluation
claim: Sleep problems that last for weeks, seriously impair daytime functioning, or involve red flags may need evaluation by a qualified professional.
practical_rule: If the user reports persistent insomnia, severe daytime sleepiness, loud snoring or breathing pauses, panic-like awakenings, major mood changes, dependence on alcohol or sedatives or stimulants, or major functional impairment, recommend professional help clearly and calmly.
when_to_use: Use for red-flag symptoms, prolonged sleep difficulty, possible sleep-disordered breathing, strong substance reliance, or major daily impairment.
avoid_advising: Do not diagnose the cause, do not provide medication instructions, and do not bury the recommendation under routine sleep-hygiene tips.

title: Breathing-related sleep symptoms should not be treated like routine sleep hygiene issues
claim: Loud snoring, gasping, choking, or reported breathing pauses during sleep can be signs that warrant medical evaluation.
practical_rule: If the user mentions gasping, choking, loud snoring, or a partner noticing breathing pauses, recommend professional evaluation and keep advice general.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports choking, gasping, breathing pauses, or strong concern about sleep-disordered breathing.
avoid_advising: Do not diagnose sleep apnea and do not frame this as a routine bedtime habit issue.

title: Severe daytime sleepiness can be a safety problem
claim: Severe sleepiness that affects driving, work, study, or normal functioning deserves caution and may need professional evaluation.
practical_rule: If the user is too sleepy to function safely, advise against driving or risky activity and recommend professional help if this is more than a one-off rough day.
when_to_use: Use when the user describes severe sleepiness, near-misses, or impaired daytime functioning.
avoid_advising: Do not tell the user to push through dangerous sleepiness for schedule optimization.

title: Sleep difficulty lasting weeks deserves more than routine troubleshooting
claim: Persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep for weeks may deserve professional evaluation rather than endless self-experimentation.
practical_rule: If the user reports insomnia or serious sleep difficulty lasting weeks, recommend a qualified clinician while still offering safe general habits.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions insomnia or sleep difficulty lasting multiple weeks.
avoid_advising: Do not diagnose insomnia and do not offer medication instructions or prescriptive treatment plans.

title: Relying on alcohol or sedatives for sleep is a red flag
claim: Needing alcohol, sedatives, sleeping pills, or similar substances to sleep can be a sign that the issue needs professional support.
practical_rule: If the user relies on alcohol or sedatives to sleep, respond supportively, do not recommend those strategies, and suggest professional help.
when_to_use: Use when the user says they need alcohol, sedatives, sleeping pills, or similar substances to sleep or wake.
avoid_advising: Do not recommend alcohol as a sleep aid and do not give medication or supplement dosing advice.

title: Dangerous sleepiness while driving needs immediate safety-first advice
claim: If the user may fall asleep while driving or operating machinery, immediate safety matters more than schedule optimization.
practical_rule: Tell the user not to drive while dangerously sleepy and to choose a safer alternative or immediate support.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions almost falling asleep while driving or needing to drive while dangerously sleepy.
avoid_advising: Do not optimize wake-up timing or caffeine strategy ahead of immediate driving safety.

title: Self-harm or suicide language is an immediate safety issue
claim: If the user mentions self-harm, suicide, or not wanting to live, the response should prioritize immediate support rather than sleep optimization.
practical_rule: Encourage immediate local emergency or crisis support and reaching out to a nearby trusted person. Keep the response calm and direct.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions self-harm, suicidal thoughts, or crisis-level hopelessness.
avoid_advising: Do not continue routine sleep coaching or optimization advice in the same response.

title: Medication-related sleep concerns should stay general and non-prescriptive
claim: Medication effects on sleep can vary, so concerns about sleep disruption or dosing are best discussed with a qualified clinician or pharmacist.
practical_rule: If the user asks whether medication is affecting sleep or asks about doses, avoid giving medication instructions and suggest professional guidance.
when_to_use: Use when the user connects sleep problems to medicine, dosage, stimulants, sedatives, or sleep aids.
avoid_advising: Do not tell the user to start, stop, raise, lower, or combine medications or supplements.
